# Editor comments

After a round of revisions, both reviewers agree that the manuscript has greatly improved, but there are still some issues that need to be addressed by the authors.
-Rongji Mu

# Response to the Editor

We would like to thank the editor and the two reviewers for their time and careful reading of our manuscript.
We believe that their valuable feedback and the revisions we made in response have substantially improved our work.
Below we respond to each point; the revised manuscript text is quoted verbatim.

# Reviewer 1
The authors have adequately addressed my previous comments, and the manuscript has been substantially improved.
I only have one minor comment.

### Minor comments

<!-- R1 C1 -->
::: {.comment}
The statement in the Abstract that “frequentist meta-analytic approaches ... often fall short in this regard” seems somewhat unbalanced. I suggest revising this statement to present a more objective comparison between frequentist and Bayesian approaches.
:::

::: {.reply}
We thank the reviewer for this comment and agree that our original statement in the abstract was unbalanced.
We have revised the paragraph.
:::

::: {.revision section="Abstract - Background"}
"Uncertainty quantification is central to evidence synthesis for risk assessment and policy-making.
Frequentist meta-analysis - currently predominant in epidemiology - quantifies uncertainty through confidence intervals, while Bayesian meta-analysis provides a different approach to uncertainty quantification through posterior distributions.
We performed frequentist and Bayesian meta-analyses to compare uncertainty quantification and applicability for risk assessment using lead exposure and children's IQ as a case study."
:::

# Reviewer 2

### Major comments

<!-- R2 C1 -->
:::{.comment}
Please address the omitted request for frequentist prediction intervals and Bayesian posterior predictive intervals, particularly given the very high heterogeneity and the manuscript's focus on uncertainty quantification.
:::

::: {.reply}
We have now added frequentist and Bayesian predictive intervals to the manuscript and revised the methods, results, and discussion accordingly.
We thank the reviewer for suggesting this addition and agree that it's an important addition to our manuscript.
We have also refocused the aims of our study in this direction (see also our response to reviewer 1, comment 1).
:::

::: {.revision section="Methods -- Bayesian Meta-Analysis"}
To quantify uncertainty in the pooled mean and heterogeneity jointly, we constructed the posterior predictive distribution of hypothetical future studies by sampling from $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \tau)$.
Additionally, a sensitivity analysis with alternative priors was conducted, as described below.
:::

::: {.revision section="Methods -- Frequentist Meta-Analysis"}
In the frequentist approach, we constructed the predictive distribution of hypothetical future studies via parametric simulation.
To enable parametric simulation from point estimates, we assumed $\mu$ to be normally distributed and $\tau$ to be log-normally distributed, sampled from these distributions, and then used these samples to draw from the predictive distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \tau)$.
The number of draws in the parametric simulation matched the number of MCMC samples from the Bayesian approach.
:::


::: {.revision section="Results"}
The Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis yielded a posterior mean pooled estimate of `r Bayes_mean` (95% credible interval (CrI): `r Bayes_lb` to `r Bayes_ub`) IQ points per log-unit increase in BLL (µg/dL) (see Fig. 2) and a 95% predictive interval from `r frnd(bayes_ppi$theta_new_q025)` to `r frnd(bayes_ppi$theta_new_q975)`.
The frequentist approach produced a comparable pooled estimate of `r freq_mean` (95% confidence interval (CI): `r freq_lb` to `r freq_ub`) and a comparable 95% predictive interval from `r frnd(freq_ppi$theta_new_q025)` to `r frnd(freq_ppi$theta_new_q975)`.
:::

::: {.revision section="Discussion"}
These predictive distributions are, however, not exclusive to the Bayesian approach.
In the frequentist framework, they can be obtained using, for example, parametric simulation, nonparametric bootstrap, or the delta method.
Each methods comes with its own assumptions that may impact the results, thus requiring the researcher to make a decision.
To illustrate this, we opted for parametric simulation because the calculations were similar to the Bayesian approach and because our small sample size made nonparametric bootstrap unfeasible, frequently leading to convergence issues.
Next, we assumed normal and log-normal distributions for $\mu$ and $\tau$, respectively, but we could have also assumed a normal distribution restricted to positive values for $\tau$ – under this assumption, the predictive intervals would have reached from `r freq_ppi$theta_new_alt_q025` to `r freq_ppi$theta_new_alt_q975`.
A notable difference to the Bayesian approach is that the data have no option to overrule the assumed distributions whereas, given sufficient data, Bayesian priors will converge to the true distribution so long as that prior places non-zero probability on the true values, which is almost always feasible in practice.
:::

<!-- R2 C2 -->
:::{.comment}
Please address the previously raised systematic-review concern, especially the literature search ending in July 2023 and the use of a single human reviewer for full-text screening/RoB assessment. (One of prior comments: The literature search ended in July 2023, although the manuscript includes references from 2025 and appears to have been prepared later. The search should be updated.)
:::

::: {.reply}
We thank the reviewer for this comment and agree that the search should be updated.
We have conducted a rapid update search in PubMed for the period from July 2023 to 2 September 2026, using the original search terms. 
Titles were screened by one reviewer and, in addition, by the LLM Claude Opus 5.
If the two judgements diverged, the record was revisited by the researcher, who made the final decision.
The search returned 173 records, and no record met the PECOTS and eligibility criteria.
No study was therefore added and the pooled estimates are unchanged.
The update is now reported in the Methods, the Results and the Discussion and the screening decisions are documented in additional file 3.
Because the update was narrower in scope than the original search, covering one database and relying on a single reviewer, we also stated in the Discussion that we cannot rule out that a full update would have identified further studies.
On the second part of the comment: we have made the limitation of having a single reviewer for the full-text screening and the RoB assessment explicit in the limitations paragraph.
We have also added that the meta-analysis rests on a restricted rather than an exhaustive evidence base and should not be read as a comprehensive evidence synthesis of the literature on lead and children's IQ.
This reviewer comment also helped us realise that the main objective of our study, which is the comparison of uncertainty quantification in frequentist and Bayesian meta-analysis, was not stated clearly enough.
We have therefore revised the aims statement at the end of the Background, the opening sentence of the Discussion and the Conclusions.
:::

::: {.revision section="Background"}
"The aim of this study is to compare uncertainty quantification of frequentist and Bayesian meta-analyses.
We apply both meta-analytic approaches to the association between BLL and IQ scores in children using the results of a systematic review on epidemiological studies published between January 2005 and July 2023, thereby also providing an updated pooled effect estimate of this association."
:::

::: {.revision section="Methods -- Literature Review"}
"The search was updated in September 2026 by a PubMed search, using the same queries as in the original search and restricted to records published after July 2023.
Titles were first screened by one reviewer and then additionally by the large language model (LLM) Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic), which was prompted to classify records using the PECOTS criteria.
If the judgement of the researcher and the LLM deviated, the record was revisited by the researcher, who made the final decision.
Where necessary, abstracts and full texts were assessed."
:::

::: {.revision section="Results -- Literature Review"}
"The update search in PubMed yielded 173 records published after July 2023.
No record met both the PECOTS and the meta-analysis eligibility criteria.
40 and 44 records were excluded because the outcome or exposure definition did not match, respectively; 30 records were excluded because the record was a review rather than a primary study and 59 records were excluded for other reasons, including the record being an animal study or focusing on the mechanisms of lead neurotoxicity.
Therefore, no new studies were added.
Screening decisions for the update are documented in additional file 3."
:::

::: {.revision section="Discussion"}
"In this study, we compare uncertainty quantification of a frequentist and a Bayesian meta-analysis, which is less used in the field of environmental epidemiology to date, using lead exposure and children's IQ as an applied example."\
"A first set of limitations concerns the evidence base underlying the pooled estimate.
Our original literature search was limited to the period between January 2005 and July 2023 and was updated in September 2026 through a single-reviewer search in PubMed, which identified no additional eligible studies.
Because this update had a narrower scope than the original search, we cannot rule out that a full update covering both databases would have identified new studies.
Both the full-text screening and RoB assessment were done by only one person; while it would have been preferable to have multiple persons screen full texts and assess RoB independently, this was not feasible in this study due to resource constraints.
We further excluded studies that did not report effect estimates on the logarithmic scale of BLL.
While this reduced the number of studies available for pooling, exclusion was necessary to ensure interpretability, as combining effect estimates expressed on different scales would render the pooled estimate uninterpretable.
The studies we did include were heterogeneous with respect to covariate adjustment, exposure range, IQ measurement instrument and cohort characteristics, meaning that the coefficients pooled in this study may not represent exactly the same estimand.
Finally, publication bias was assessed through visual inspection only; formal statistical testing, such as Egger's test, would provide a more rigorous evaluation.
The visual assessment did not rule out publication bias, which may have led to overestimation of the pooled effect.

Taken together, these limitations mean that the pooled estimate rests on a restricted rather than an exhaustive evidence base.
This study should therefore not be interpreted as a comprehensive evidence synthesis of the literature on lead and children's IQ.
Given our study's primary focus on comparing uncertainty quantification in two meta-analytic frameworks, however, these limitations do not affect our main conclusions."
:::

::: {.revision section="Conclusion"}
"This study provides an applied methodological comparison of Bayesian and frequentist meta-analysis and an evidence synthesis of epidemiological studies examining the association between lead exposure and children's IQ."
:::
